\section{Setup and basic selection geometry}\label{sec:setup}

\begin{definition}[attention row]
An \emph{attention row} on $n$ keys is $p=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ with $p_i\ge 0$ and
$\sum_i p_i = 1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[captured mass]
For $k\in\mathbb{N}$, the admissible width-$k$ selections are the key sets $S$ with
$\lvert S\rvert\le k$, and
\[
M(k)=\max_{\lvert S\rvert\le k}\ \sum_{i\in S}p_i .
\]
The maximum is over a nonempty finite family ($S=\emptyset$ is admissible), so $M$ is well
defined and $M(0)=0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[effective support]
$\eff(p)=1/\sum_i p_i^{2}$, the participation ratio; $1\le\eff(p)\le n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[selection gap]
$G(k)=M(k)-k/n$. Proposition \ref{prop:expmass} justifies the subtracted term.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[cost and speedup]
The cost of top-$k$ causal attention at context $\ctx$ is $\ctx\cdot k$ score evaluations,
and $\spd(\ctx,k)=\ctx/k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[selection optimality]\label{prop:opt}
For every $S$ with $\lvert S\rvert\le k$ we have $\sum_{i\in S}p_i\le M(k)$; consequently
$0\le M(k)\le 1$ and $M$ is nondecreasing.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from the definition of $M$ as a maximum over a family growing with $k$;
$M(k)\le 1$ since the weights are nonnegative and sum to one.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[strict improvement by swap]
If $\lvert S\rvert\le k$, $j\in S$, $i\notin S$ and $p_i>p_j$, then
$\sum_{x\in S}p_x<M(k)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
$S'=(S\setminus\{j\})\cup\{i\}$ is admissible and carries mass
$\sum_{x\in S}p_x+(p_i-p_j)$; apply Proposition \ref{prop:opt}.
\end{proof}

\section{Two-sided bounds on the knee}\label{sec:twosided}

\subsection{The concentration floor}

\begin{theorem}[Chebyshev bound on selected mass]\label{thm:cheb}
For every $k$, $\;M(k)^{2}\le k\sum_i p_i^{2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $S$ attain the maximum. Cauchy--Schwarz gives
$\bigl(\sum_{i\in S}p_i\bigr)^{2}\le\lvert S\rvert\sum_{i\in S}p_i^{2}$; enlarge the second
sum to all indices and replace $\lvert S\rvert$ by $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[concentration floor]\label{thm:floor}
If $\tau\ge 0$ and $M(k)\ge\tau$, then $k\ge\tau^{2}\eff(p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Square the hypothesis and combine with Theorem \ref{thm:cheb} to get
$\tau^{2}\le k\sum_i p_i^{2}$; divide by $\sum_i p_i^{2}>0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:183}
With $\eff(p)=216.92$, any width reaching mass $0.92$ satisfies $k>183$, since
$0.92^{2}\cdot 216.92>183$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[the square is necessary]
Let $q=(\tfrac12,\tfrac18,\tfrac18,\tfrac18,\tfrac18)$. Then $\sum_i q_i^{2}=\tfrac{5}{16}$,
so $\eff(q)=\tfrac{16}{5}$, and $M(1)=\tfrac12$. At $\tau=\tfrac12$, $k=1$:
\[
\tau^{2}\eff(q)=\tfrac45\le 1=k,\qquad \tau\,\eff(q)=\tfrac85>1=k .
\]
Hence Theorem \ref{thm:floor} cannot be strengthened by replacing $\tau^{2}$ with $\tau$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[the floor is loose on flat rows]
For the uniform row on $n$ keys, $M(k)=k/n$ for $k\le n$ and $\eff=n$. The true minimal
width for target $\tau$ is $\lceil\tau n\rceil$, while the floor certifies only
$\tau^{2}n$: a slack factor $1/\tau$.
\end{theorem}

\subsection{The tail ceiling}

\begin{lemma}[tangent-line step]\label{lem:tangent}
For $\alpha>1$ and $x\ge 1$,
\[
(\alpha-1)(x+1)^{-\alpha}\ \le\ x^{1-\alpha}-(x+1)^{1-\alpha}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The right-hand side equals $\int_x^{x+1}(\alpha-1)t^{-\alpha}\,dt$ and $t\mapsto t^{-\alpha}$
is decreasing, so the integral is at least $(\alpha-1)(x+1)^{-\alpha}$. Equivalently, and
without integration, this is Bernoulli's inequality $1+\alpha s\le(1+s)^{\alpha}$ at
$s=1/x$: convexity of $t\mapsto t^{1-\alpha}$ supplies the slack that exact telescoping
provides for free only at $\alpha=2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[power-tail sum bound]\label{lem:tailsum}
For $\alpha>1$ and $1\le k\le n$,
$\;\sum_{j=k}^{n-1}(j+1)^{-\alpha}\le \dfrac{k^{1-\alpha}}{\alpha-1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Divide Lemma \ref{lem:tangent} by $\alpha-1$ and telescope over $x=k,\dots,n-1$, obtaining
$\frac{1}{\alpha-1}(k^{1-\alpha}-n^{1-\alpha})\le\frac{k^{1-\alpha}}{\alpha-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[mass bound under a power tail]\label{thm:powermass}
Suppose the keys can be ranked by a permutation $\sigma$ so that
$p_{\sigma(i)}\le c\,(i+1)^{-\alpha}$ for $i=0,\dots,n-1$, with $c\ge 0$, $\alpha>1$. Then
for $k\ge1$,
\[
M(k)\ \ge\ 1-\frac{c}{\alpha-1}\,k^{1-\alpha}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $S$ be the set of keys of rank $<k$; then $\lvert S\rvert\le k$ and
$M(k)\ge 1-\sum_{i\notin S}p_i$, and the omitted weight is at most
$c\sum_{j=k}^{n-1}(j+1)^{-\alpha}\le\frac{c}{\alpha-1}k^{1-\alpha}$ by Lemma
\ref{lem:tailsum}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[tail ceiling on the knee]\label{thm:ceiling}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{thm:powermass} and for $\tau<1$, every width $k\ge1$
with $k\ge\bigl(\frac{c}{(\alpha-1)(1-\tau)}\bigr)^{1/(\alpha-1)}$ satisfies $M(k)\ge\tau$;
hence the knee obeys the same upper bound. For $\alpha=2$ this reads $k^{*}\le c/(1-\tau)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[instances at $n=512$]
An inverse-square tail with $c=20$ gives $M(256)\ge 1-20/256\ge 0.92$; the heavier tail
$\alpha=3/2$, $c=0.6$ gives $M(256)\ge 1-1.2/16=0.925\ge 0.92$. Both certify the measured
top-$256$ mass $0.922$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[two-sided knee law]
Fix $\tau\in[0,1)$ and assume a power tail with constant $c$ and exponent $\alpha>1$. Then
\[
\tau^{2}\eff(p)\ \le\ k^{*}(\tau)\ \le\
\Bigl(\frac{c}{(\alpha-1)(1-\tau)}\Bigr)^{1/(\alpha-1)} .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[comparison principle]
If $M_p(k)\ge M_q(k)$ for all $k$, then for every target the knee of $p$ is at most that of
$q$: more concentrated rows have smaller knees.
\end{theorem}

\section{The random control and the selection gap}\label{sec:control}

\begin{proposition}[expected mass of a random width-$k$ selection]\label{prop:expmass}
For $1\le k\le n$, averaging over the $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size exactly $k$, chosen
uniformly,
\[
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sum_{i\in R}p_i\Bigr]=\frac{k}{n}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Sum captured mass over all $k$-subsets and exchange summation: each key lies in
$\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ of them, so the total is $\binom{n-1}{k-1}\sum_i p_i=\binom{n-1}{k-1}$.
Divide by $\binom{n}{k}$ and use $\binom{n-1}{k-1}/\binom{n}{k}=k/n$.
\end{proof}

The identity is exact and distribution-free: the control's expected mass does not depend on
$p$, which is what makes it a legitimate baseline.

\begin{corollary}
$M(k)\ge k/n$ for $1\le k\le n$, i.e.\ $G(k)\ge0$: a maximum is at least an average. At
$(n,k)=(512,256)$ the control captures exactly $\tfrac12$, so measured $M(256)\ge0.922$
yields a mass gap of at least $0.42$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{Concavity by exchange}

\begin{theorem}[concavity of the mass curve]\label{thm:concave}
For every $k\ge0$, $\;M(k+2)+M(k)\le 2M(k+1)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose optimal $S$ ($\lvert S\rvert\le k+2$) and $T$ ($\lvert T\rvert\le k$).
If $\lvert S\rvert\le k+1$, both sets are admissible at width $k+1$ and the claim follows by
adding two instances of Proposition \ref{prop:opt}. Otherwise $\lvert S\rvert=k+2>\lvert
T\rvert$, so there is $x\in S\setminus T$. The sets $S\setminus\{x\}$ and $T\cup\{x\}$ have
cardinalities at most $k+1$ and total mass
$\bigl(\sum_S p-p_x\bigr)+\bigl(p_x+\sum_T p\bigr)=M(k+2)+M(k)$; each summand is at most
$M(k+1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
$f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a \emph{concave sequence} if $f(k+2)+f(k)\le 2f(k+1)$ for all
$k$.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}
$M$ is a concave sequence, and so is $G(k)=M(k)-k/n$, since subtracting an affine function
preserves the defining inequality.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[antitone increments]\label{lem:antitone}
If $f$ is concave then $k\mapsto f(k+1)-f(k)$ is nonincreasing.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[telescoping]\label{lem:tele}
$f(m+t)=f(m)+\sum_{s<t}\bigl(f(m+s+1)-f(m+s)\bigr)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[chord comparison]\label{lem:chord}
If $f$ is concave and $i\le j$, then $f(j+t)-f(j)\le f(i+t)-f(i)$ for every $t\ge0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write both sides as sums of $t$ increments (Lemma \ref{lem:tele}) and compare termwise via
Lemma \ref{lem:antitone}, using $i+s\le j+s$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[concave $\Rightarrow$ unimodal]\label{thm:unimodal}
If $f$ is concave and $i\le j\le m$, then $\min\bigl(f(i),f(m)\bigr)\le f(j)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $f(i)\le f(j)$ we are done. Otherwise some increment on $[i,j)$ is negative (else
telescoping would give $f(i)\le f(j)$); by Lemma \ref{lem:antitone} all increments from that
index on are nonpositive, in particular on $[j,m)$, so $f(m)\le f(j)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[shape of the gap]
$G$ is concave, hence unimodal. Moreover $G(0)=0$ and $G(n)=0$, so $G(k)\ge0$ for
$0\le k\le n$: nonnegativity of the selection gap follows from shape alone, independently of
the averaging argument.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[chord extrapolation]\label{thm:chordpred}
Let $f$ be any concave sequence with $f(256)=2.6$ and $f(384)=1.7$. Then $f(512)\le0.8$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lemma \ref{lem:chord} with $i=256$, $j=384$, $t=128$ gives
$f(512)-f(384)\le f(384)-f(256)=-0.9$.
\end{proof}

Applied to the measured accuracy gaps $+2.6$ and $+1.7$, this predicts a gap of at most
$+0.8$ at full width; a larger measured value would refute concavity of the accuracy gap.
For the mass gap, concavity is unconditional by Theorem \ref{thm:concave}.

\section{Where the peak sits: total variation}\label{sec:peak}

\begin{definition}
$A=\{i:p_i>1/n\}$ (the above-average keys) and
$E(p)=\sum_i\bigl(p_i-\tfrac1n\bigr)^{+}$ (the excess mass).
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[excess mass is total variation]
$E(p)=\tfrac12\sum_i\lvert p_i-\tfrac1n\rvert=\TV(p,\unif)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The signed deviations sum to $0$, so total positive and negative parts coincide; each is
half the $\ell^{1}$ deviation.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:disc}
For every key set $S$, $\;\sum_{i\in S}p_i-\lvert S\rvert/n\le E(p)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[width-free ceiling on the gap]\label{thm:cap}
For every $k$, $\;G(k)\le E(p)=\TV(p,\unif)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $S$ attains $M(k)$ then $\lvert S\rvert\le k$ and
$G(k)\le\sum_{i\in S}p_i-\lvert S\rvert/n\le E(p)$ by Lemma \ref{lem:disc}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[the peak, exactly]
$G(\lvert A\rvert)=E(p)$; hence $G$ attains its maximum at $k=\lvert A\rvert$, with value
$\TV(p,\unif)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Off $A$ the positive part vanishes, so
$E(p)=\sum_{i\in A}p_i-\lvert A\rvert/n\le M(\lvert A\rvert)-\lvert A\rvert/n
=G(\lvert A\rvert)$, since $A$ is admissible at width $\lvert A\rvert$; the reverse
inequality is Theorem \ref{thm:cap}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[the peak is interior]
$\lvert A\rvert<n$: if every key exceeded $1/n$ the weights would sum to more than $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[total-variation floor on the knee]
If $M(k)\ge\tau$ then $k\ge n\bigl(\tau-\TV(p,\unif)\bigr)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
With $n=512$ and $M(256)\ge0.922$, Theorem \ref{thm:cap} forces
$\TV(p,\unif)\ge0.922-\tfrac12=0.422$.
\end{corollary}

\section{From captured mass to accuracy}

\begin{theorem}[concavity transfer]
If $f$ is a concave sequence and $g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is concave and nondecreasing,
then $k\mapsto g(f(k))$ is a concave sequence.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Concavity of $f$ gives $\tfrac12 f(k+2)+\tfrac12 f(k)\le f(k+1)$; monotonicity of $g$ then
gives $g\bigl(\tfrac12 f(k+2)+\tfrac12 f(k)\bigr)\le g(f(k+1))$, while concavity of $g$
gives $\tfrac12 g(f(k+2))+\tfrac12 g(f(k))\le g\bigl(\tfrac12 f(k+2)+\tfrac12 f(k)\bigr)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If accuracy is a concave nondecreasing function $g$ of captured mass, then $k\mapsto
g(M(k))$ is concave, hence unimodal, with nonincreasing increments: each additional unit of
width buys no more than the previous one. This is exactly the shape a knee sweep
presupposes.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Lipschitz ceiling on the accuracy gap]
If $g(x)-g(y)\le L(x-y)$ for $y\le x$ with $L\ge0$, then for every $k\le n$,
\[
g\bigl(M(k)\bigr)-g\bigl(k/n\bigr)\ \le\ L\cdot\TV(p,\unif).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$k/n\le M(k)$, so the Lipschitz hypothesis bounds the left side by $L\,G(k)$; apply Theorem
\ref{thm:cap}.
\end{proof}

\section{The measurement protocol}\label{sec:protocol}

\begin{definition}
A predicate $P$ on widths is \emph{upward closed} if $P(a)$ and $a\le b$ imply $P(b)$. Given
that some width passes, the \emph{knee} is $\min\{k:P(k)\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}
If $r$ is a nondecreasing accuracy curve then $P(k)\equiv(r(k)\ge\mathrm{bar})$ is upward
closed.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[bracket lemma]\label{thm:bracket}
If $P$ is upward closed, $\neg P(a)$ and $P(b)$, then the knee lies in $(a,b]$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}
On $\mathcal{G}=\{96,128,160,192,224,240,256,288,320,384,512\}$, the only element of
$(240,256]$ is $256$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[two-seed exact agreement]
Let two runs have upward-closed pass predicates whose knees are grid points. If both fail at
$240$ and pass at $256$, then both knees equal $256$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[grid resolution]\label{thm:res}
Let $a<b$ be consecutive grid points with $b\le\rho a$, $\rho\ge1$, and let the true knee $k$
satisfy $a<k\le b$. Then $\lvert b-k\rvert\le(1-1/\rho)b$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}
With $a=240$, $b=256$, $\rho=16/15$, a knee reported as $256$ carries at most $16$ of
absolute uncertainty, and two seeds bracketed in $(240,256]$ differ by strictly less than
$16$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[the resolution bound is attained]
For $a<b$ let $r(k)=\mathbf{1}[k>a]$. Then $r$ is nondecreasing, fails at $a$, passes at $b$,
and its true knee is $a+1$. A grid containing $a$ and $b$ but nothing between can only
report $b$, so the residual uncertainty $b-a-1$ is realised exactly.
\end{theorem}

\section{The depth law}

\begin{definition}
$k^{*}_{\text{law}}(d)=C\,d^{2/3}$, with fitted constant $C=24.7$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
For $C\ge0$ the law is concave on $[0,\infty)$ and subadditive:
$k^{*}_{\text{law}}(d_1+d_2)\le k^{*}_{\text{law}}(d_1)+k^{*}_{\text{law}}(d_2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[per-doubling factor]
$k^{*}_{\text{law}}(2d)=2^{2/3}k^{*}_{\text{law}}(d)$ and $1.58<2^{2/3}<1.59<2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Homogeneity gives the identity. Cubing, $(2^{2/3})^{3}=4$ while $1.58^{3}<4<1.59^{3}$;
monotonicity of cubing transfers the bounds, and $2^{3}=8>4$ gives $2^{2/3}<2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[affine extrapolation over-predicts]
Let $f$ be concave and let $\ell$ be the affine function agreeing with $f$ at $d_1<d_2$.
Then $f(d)\le\ell(d)$ for every $d>d_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $d_2=\lambda d_1+(1-\lambda)d$ with $\lambda=(d-d_2)/(d-d_1)\in(0,1)$. Concavity gives
$f(d_2)\ge\lambda f(d_1)+(1-\lambda)f(d)$; solving for $f(d)$ yields $f(d)\le\ell(d)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$32^{2/3}\in(10.079,10.080)$, so $24.7\cdot 32^{2/3}\in(248.9,249)$: within $3\%$ of the
measured knee $256$. The affine model $8d+32$ predicts $288>1.11\cdot256$, an
over-prediction exceeding $11\%$ that is structurally forced; the product law $k^{*}=\ctx$
over-predicts by a factor of $2$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[empirical exponent bracket]
The measured per-doubling ratios $1.50,1.58,1.68$ have product $3.9816$. If $2^{3a}=3.9816$
then $0.6<a<2/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$3.9816<4=2^{2}$ gives $3a<2$. For the lower bound, $\bigl(2^{9/5}\bigr)^{5}=512$ while
$3.98^{5}>512$, so $2^{9/5}<3.9816$ and $3a>9/5$.
\end{proof}

\section{Cost arithmetic}

\begin{theorem}
With $\spd(\ctx,k)=\ctx/k$: (a) the product-law prescription $k=\ctx$ gives $\spd=1$; (b)
$\spd(512,256)=2$ exactly; (c) any knee with $2k\le\ctx$ gives $\spd\ge2$.
\end{theorem}

The distinction between a knee at $256$ and a knee at $512$ is exactly the distinction
between a $2.0\times$ saving and none, and Corollary \ref{cor:183} rules out any wishful
knee below $184$ at this cell.

\section{Algorithms}

\textbf{A. Mass curve and gap.} Sort the row descending, take prefix sums to obtain $M$, and
subtract $k/n$ to obtain $G$: $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ space. Concavity of $M$ and the peak
location $\lvert A\rvert$ are testable invariants of the output.

\textbf{B. Certified knee bracket.} Given a monotone pass oracle and a grid, binary search
for the least passing grid point $b$ and its predecessor $a$; report the bracket $(a,b]$ and
the resolution $(1-1/\rho)b$ with $\rho=b/a$ (Theorems \ref{thm:bracket}, \ref{thm:res}).
Cost: $O(\log\lvert\mathcal{G}\rvert)$ oracle calls.

\textbf{C. Two-sided sandwich.} Compute $\eff$ and the floor $\tau^{2}\eff$; fit a power tail
$(c,\alpha)$ to the sorted weights and compute the ceiling
$\bigl(\frac{c}{(\alpha-1)(1-\tau)}\bigr)^{1/(\alpha-1)}$; report the interval.

\section{Discussion and limitations}

The theory is exact and assumption-light but concerns a single attention row, whereas a model
has many rows, heads and layers. Bridging to accuracy uses the monotone concave response
hypothesis, a modelling assumption rather than a theorem; we have stated which results depend
on it and which do not. The empirical numbers are small-scale measurements; mathematics
contributes their interpretation --- which features are structurally constrained (sign of the
gap, shape of the curve, bracket arithmetic, over-prediction of affine extrapolation) and
which are free (the constant $C$, the tail parameters, the bar). Finally, reporting a knee of
$256$ from a grid of local ratio $16/15$ means honestly $k^{*}\in(240,256]$, and this cannot
be sharpened without a finer grid.

\section{Future directions}

Sharper tail models (stretched-exponential, log-normal) should yield to the same tangent-line
technique. A multi-row theory would study the aggregate gap $\sum_r G_r(k)$, concave termwise
but with a peak governed by an averaged total-variation distance. The width-free cap
$\TV(p,\unif)$ applies to every selection scheme and is attained by top-$k$ at
$k=\lvert A\rvert$; quantifying the shortfall off the peak would delimit when a cheaper
approximate selector loses nothing. Extending the depth ladder tests whether the exponent
drifts from $2/3$. Finally, the chord bound of Theorem \ref{thm:chordpred} predicts an
accuracy gap of at most $+0.8$ at full width --- a cheap, direct test of the response
hypothesis.

\section{Conclusion}

Cauchy--Schwarz floors the knee at $\tau^{2}$ times the participation ratio, with the square
provably necessary; a discrete tangent-line estimate ceilings it under any power tail with
exponent above one; a double count makes the random control exactly $k/n$; and a one-step
exchange makes the mass curve concave, whence unimodality, nonnegativity of the selection
gap, diminishing returns and a falsifiable chord bound. The gap peaks exactly at the
above-average keys with height equal to the total-variation distance to uniform, which caps
the accuracy advantage of any selection scheme under a Lipschitz response. At the deepest
measured rung the knee is $256$ at two seeds, the concentration floor forces it above $183$,
the rows lie at distance at least $0.422$ from uniform, the concave law predicts $249$, the
affine alternative over-predicts by more than $11\%$ of necessity, the product law delivers
no speedup at all, and the measured knee delivers exactly $2.0\times$.

\end{document}

  "demo": """"
Numerical demonstrations for
"The Geometry of Attention Sparsification: Concentration Floors, Tail Ceilings,
and the Concavity of the Selection Gap".

Self-contained: standard library only (math, random, itertools, fractions).

An attention row is a probability vector p on n keys.  We study

    M(k) = max_{|S| <= k} sum_{i in S} p_i        (top-k captured mass)
    G(k) = M(k) - k/n                             (selection gap)
    eff  = 1 / sum_i p_i^2                        (participation ratio)

and verify, numerically, each theorem of the paper:

  1. concentration floor              k >= tau^2 * eff
  2. sharpness of the square          spike profile refutes k >= tau * eff
  3. power-tail ceiling               M(k) >= 1 - c/(alpha-1) * k^(1-alpha)
  4. exact random control             E[mass of random k-set] = k/n
  5. concavity by exchange            M(k+2) + M(k) <= 2 M(k+1)
  6. unimodality of the gap           min(G(i), G(m)) <= G(j) for i <= j <= m
  7. peak location and height         argmax G = |{i : p_i > 1/n}|, max G = TV(p, unif)
  8. Lipschitz accuracy ceiling       g(M(k)) - g(k/n) <= L * TV
  9. knee brackets and grid resolution
 10. depth law arithmetic and speedup
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core quantities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normalize(w: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Turn a nonnegative weight vector into an attention row (sums to 1)."""
    total = float(sum(w))
    if total <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("weights must have positive total")
    return [float(x) / total for x in w]


def mass_curve(p: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """M(0), M(1), ..., M(n): prefix sums of the descending sort.  O(n log n)."""
    srt = sorted(p, reverse=True)
    out = [0.0]
    acc = 0.0
    for x in srt:
        acc += x
        out.append(acc)
    return out


def best_mass(p: Sequence[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Mass captured by the best width-k selection."""
    return mass_curve(p)[min(k, len(p))]


def selection_gap_curve(p: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """G(k) = M(k) - k/n for k = 0..n."""
    n = len(p)
    return [m - k / n for k, m in enumerate(mass_curve(p))]


def eff_support(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Participation ratio eff(p) = 1 / sum_i p_i^2."""
    return 1.0 / sum(x * x for x in p)


def tv_to_uniform(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Total-variation distance between p and the uniform row."""
    n = len(p)
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(x - 1.0 / n) for x in p)


def excess_mass(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """sum_i (p_i - 1/n)^+ ; equals tv_to_uniform(p)."""
    n = len(p)
    return sum(max(x - 1.0 / n, 0.0) for x in p)


def above_average_count(p: Sequence[float]) -> int:
    """|{i : p_i > 1/n}| -- the peak width of the selection gap."""
    n = len(p)
    return sum(1 for x in p if x > 1.0 / n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Profile families
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def uniform_row(n: int) -> List[float]:
    return [1.0 / n] * n


def spike_row() -> List[float]:
    """The five-key spike profile (1/2, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8)."""
    return [0.5, 0.125, 0.125, 0.125, 0.125]


def power_row(n: int, alpha: float) -> List[float]:
    """Normalised power-law profile p_(i) proportional to (i+1)^(-alpha)."""
    return normalize([(i + 1.0) ** (-alpha) for i in range(n)])


def mixture_row(n: int, head: int, head_share: float, seed: int = 0) -> List[float]:
    """`head` keys share `head_share` of the mass; the rest is noisy background."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    w = [0.0] * n
    for i in range(head):
        w[i] = head_share / head * (0.8 + 0.4 * rng.random())
    for i in range(head, n):
        w[i] = (1.0 - head_share) / (n - head) * (0.5 + rng.random())
    return normalize(w)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1-2. Concentration floor and its sharpness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def concentration_floor(tau: float, p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Theorem: any k with M(k) >= tau obeys k >= tau^2 * eff(p)."""
    return tau * tau * eff_support(p)


def demo_concentration() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. CONCENTRATION FLOOR   k >= tau^2 * eff")
    print("=" * 74)
    for name, p in [
        ("uniform(512)", uniform_row(512)),
        ("power alpha=1.1", power_row(512, 1.1)),
        ("power alpha=2.0", power_row(512, 2.0)),
        ("mixture head=180", mixture_row(512, 180, 0.90)),
    ]:
        e = eff_support(p)
        tau = 0.92
        floor = concentration_floor(tau, p)
        curve = mass_curve(p)
        true_k = next(k for k in range(len(p) + 1) if curve[k] >= tau)
        print(
            f"  {name:>18}:  eff={e:8.2f}   floor(tau=0.92)={floor:8.2f}"
            f"   true minimal k={true_k:4d}   OK={true_k >= floor - 1e-9}"
        )

    print("\n  Measured cell (reported eff = 216.92, tau = 0.92):")
    print(f"    floor = 0.92^2 * 216.92 = {0.92 ** 2 * 216.92:.3f}  >  183"
          "   -> no width below 184 can reach mass 0.92")

    print("\n2. SHARPNESS: the square in tau^2 cannot be removed")
    q = spike_row()
    e = eff_support(q)
    print(f"    spike profile {q}")
    print(f"    eff = {e:.4f} = 16/5,   M(1) = {best_mass(q, 1):.4f} = 1/2")
    print(f"    proved floor  tau^2*eff = {0.5 ** 2 * e:.4f} <= 1   (holds)")
    print(f"    false 'floor' tau  *eff = {0.5 * e:.4f}  > 1   (would be violated)")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Power-tail ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def power_tail_mass_bound(c: float, alpha: float, k: int) -> float:
    """Guaranteed mass 1 - c/(alpha-1) * k^(1-alpha) under p_(i) <= c (i+1)^(-alpha)."""
    return 1.0 - c / (alpha - 1.0) * k ** (1.0 - alpha)


def power_tail_knee_ceiling(c: float, alpha: float, tau: float) -> float:
    """Sufficient width: (c / ((alpha-1)(1-tau)))^(1/(alpha-1))."""
    return (c / ((alpha - 1.0) * (1.0 - tau))) ** (1.0 / (alpha - 1.0))


def demo_tail_ceiling() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. POWER-TAIL CEILING   M(k) >= 1 - c/(alpha-1) k^(1-alpha)")
    print("=" * 74)
    cases = [(20.0, 2.0), (0.6, 1.5), (2.0, 1.25)]
    for c, alpha in cases:
        bound = power_tail_mass_bound(c, alpha, 256)
        ceil = power_tail_knee_ceiling(c, alpha, 0.92)
        print(f"  c={c:5.2f}, alpha={alpha:4.2f}:  certified M(256) >= {bound:6.4f}"
              f"    knee ceiling for tau=0.92: k* <= {ceil:9.2f}")

    print("\n  Verification against genuine power-law rows (n = 512):")
    for alpha in (1.5, 2.0, 3.0):
        p = power_row(512, alpha)
        # a valid majorant constant for this normalised row
        c = max(p[i] * (i + 1.0) ** alpha for i in range(512))
        bound = power_tail_mass_bound(c, alpha, 256)
        actual = best_mass(p, 256)
        print(f"    alpha={alpha:4.2f}:  fitted c={c:7.4f}   bound={bound:7.4f}"
              f"   actual M(256)={actual:7.4f}   valid={actual >= bound - 1e-12}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Exact random control
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def exact_expected_random_mass(p: Sequence[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Brute-force average of captured mass over ALL k-subsets (small n only)."""
    n = len(p)
    idx = range(n)
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    for S in itertools.combinations(idx, k):
        total += sum(p[i] for i in S)
        count += 1
    return total / count


def demo_random_control() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. RANDOM CONTROL:  E[mass of a uniformly random k-set] = k/n exactly")
    print("=" * 74)
    p = normalize([7.0, 3.0, 1.0, 0.4, 0.05, 0.02, 0.9, 2.2])
    n = len(p)
    print(f"  row (n={n}): " + ", ".join(f"{x:.4f}" for x in p))
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        emp = exact_expected_random_mass(p, k)
        print(f"    k={k}:  exact average over C({n},{k}) subsets = {emp:.12f}"
              f"   k/n = {k / n:.12f}   match={abs(emp - k / n) < 1e-12}")

    print("\n  Monte-Carlo at the measured cell (n=512, k=256, 20000 draws):")
    row = mixture_row(512, 180, 0.90)
    rng = random.Random(43)
    draws = 20000
    acc = 0.0
    for _ in range(draws):
        S = rng.sample(range(512), 256)
        acc += sum(row[i] for i in S)
    print(f"    empirical mean = {acc / draws:.6f}   theory k/n = {256 / 512:.6f}")
    print(f"    top-256 mass   = {best_mass(row, 256):.6f}"
          f"   mass gap = {best_mass(row, 256) - 0.5:.6f}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5-7. Concavity, unimodality, peak
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_concave_sequence(f: Sequence[float], tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool:
    return all(f[k + 2] + f[k] <= 2.0 * f[k + 1] + tol for k in range(len(f) - 2))


def is_unimodal(f: Sequence[float], tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool:
    """min(f[i], f[m]) <= f[j] for all i <= j <= m (checked exhaustively)."""
    n = len(f)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            for m in range(j, n):
                if min(f[i], f[m]) > f[j] + tol:
                    return False
    return True


def chord_extrapolation(f_at_i: float, f_at_j: float, i: int, j: int, t: int) -> float:
    """Concavity cap on f(j+t) given f(i), f(j) with j - i = t."""
    if j - i != t:
        raise ValueError("chord comparison needs equal step lengths")
    return f_at_j + (f_at_j - f_at_i)


def demo_shape() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("5-7. CONCAVITY, UNIMODALITY, PEAK LOCATION")
    print("=" * 74)
    rows = {
        "uniform(64)": uniform_row(64),
        "power alpha=1.5 (64)": power_row(64, 1.5),
        "spike (5)": spike_row(),
        "mixture head=20 (64)": mixture_row(64, 20, 0.85, seed=7),
    }
    for name, p in rows.items():
        M = mass_curve(p)
        G = selection_gap_curve(p)
        peak_k = max(range(len(G)), key=lambda k: G[k])
        print(f"  {name:>22}: M concave={is_concave_sequence(M)}"
              f"  G concave={is_concave_sequence(G)}"
              f"  G unimodal={is_unimodal(G)}")
        print(f"      argmax G = {peak_k:3d}   |above-average keys| = "
              f"{above_average_count(p):3d}   max G = {G[peak_k]:.6f}"
              f"   TV = {tv_to_uniform(p):.6f}   excess = {excess_mass(p):.6f}")
        print(f"      G(0) = {G[0]:.1e}   G(n) = {G[-1]:.1e}   min G = {min(G):.1e}")

    print("\n  Chord extrapolation of the measured accuracy gaps:")
    cap = chord_extrapolation(2.6, 1.7, 256, 384, 128)
    print(f"    gap(256)=+2.6, gap(384)=+1.7  =>  gap(512) <= {cap:.2f}"
          "   (concavity; measured value above this refutes it)")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 8. Accuracy transfer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def demo_accuracy_transfer() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. ACCURACY TRANSFER:  concave response, Lipschitz ceiling L * TV")
    print("=" * 74)
    p = mixture_row(512, 180, 0.90, seed=11)
    M = mass_curve(p)
    scale, rate = 0.15, 3.0  # accuracy scale and saturation rate

    def g(x: float) -> float:
        """Concave nondecreasing response g(x) = scale * (1 - exp(-rate x)).

        Its derivative scale*rate*exp(-rate x) is positive and decreasing, so g is
        nondecreasing, concave, and Lipschitz with constant L = scale * rate.
        """
        x = min(max(x, 0.0), 1.0)
        return scale * (1.0 - math.exp(-rate * x))

    lipschitz = scale * rate
    acc = [g(m) for m in M]
    print(f"  response g(x) = {scale} (1 - e^(-{rate}x)): concave, nondecreasing,"
          f" L = {lipschitz:.3f}")
    print(f"  accuracy curve k -> g(M(k)) concave = {is_concave_sequence(acc)}")
    incs = [acc[k + 1] - acc[k] for k in range(len(acc) - 1)]
    print("  increments nonincreasing (diminishing returns) = "
          f"{all(incs[k + 1] <= incs[k] + 1e-12 for k in range(len(incs) - 1))}")
    tv = tv_to_uniform(p)
    worst = max(g(M[k]) - g(k / len(p)) for k in range(len(p) + 1))
    print(f"  TV(p, uniform) = {tv:.6f}")
    print(f"  max_k [ g(M(k)) - g(k/n) ] = {worst:.6f}"
          f"   <=  L * TV = {lipschitz * tv:.6f}   ->"
          f" {worst <= lipschitz * tv + 1e-12}")
    print(f"  width-free mass-gap cap  max_k G(k) = {max(selection_gap_curve(p)):.6f}"
          f"  (equals TV: {abs(max(selection_gap_curve(p)) - tv) < 1e-12})")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 9. Knee brackets and grid resolution
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

SWEEP_GRID: Tuple[int, ...] = (96, 128, 160, 192, 224, 240, 256, 288, 320, 384, 512)


def certified_bracket(grid: Sequence[int], passes: Callable[[int], bool]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Least passing grid point b and its predecessor a; the knee lies in (a, b]."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(grid) - 1
    if not passes(grid[hi]):
        raise ValueError("no grid point passes")
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if passes(grid[mid]):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    b = grid[lo]
    a = grid[lo - 1] if lo > 0 else 0
    return a, b


def grid_resolution(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    """(1 - 1/rho) * b with rho = b / a: the residual uncertainty of reporting b."""
    rho = b / a
    return (1.0 - 1.0 / rho) * b

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
import math
import random
from typing import Callable, Iterable, List, Sequence, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Core quantities
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def normalize(w: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Turn a nonnegative weight vector into an attention row (sums to 1)."""
    total = float(sum(w))
    if total <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("weights must have positive total")
    return [float(x) / total for x in w]


def mass_curve(p: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """M(0), M(1), ..., M(n): prefix sums of the descending sort.  O(n log n)."""
    srt = sorted(p, reverse=True)
    out = [0.0]
    acc = 0.0
    for x in srt:
        acc += x
        out.append(acc)
    return out


def best_mass(p: Sequence[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Mass captured by the best width-k selection."""
    return mass_curve(p)[min(k, len(p))]


def selection_gap_curve(p: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    """G(k) = M(k) - k/n for k = 0..n."""
    n = len(p)
    return [m - k / n for k, m in enumerate(mass_curve(p))]


def eff_support(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Participation ratio eff(p) = 1 / sum_i p_i^2."""
    return 1.0 / sum(x * x for x in p)


def tv_to_uniform(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Total-variation distance between p and the uniform row."""
    n = len(p)
    return 0.5 * sum(abs(x - 1.0 / n) for x in p)


def excess_mass(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """sum_i (p_i - 1/n)^+ ; equals tv_to_uniform(p)."""
    n = len(p)
    return sum(max(x - 1.0 / n, 0.0) for x in p)


def above_average_count(p: Sequence[float]) -> int:
    """|{i : p_i > 1/n}| -- the peak width of the selection gap."""
    n = len(p)
    return sum(1 for x in p if x > 1.0 / n)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Profile families
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def uniform_row(n: int) -> List[float]:
    return [1.0 / n] * n


def spike_row() -> List[float]:
    """The five-key spike profile (1/2, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8)."""
    return [0.5, 0.125, 0.125, 0.125, 0.125]


def power_row(n: int, alpha: float) -> List[float]:
    """Normalised power-law profile p_(i) proportional to (i+1)^(-alpha)."""
    return normalize([(i + 1.0) ** (-alpha) for i in range(n)])


def mixture_row(n: int, head: int, head_share: float, seed: int = 0) -> List[float]:
    """`head` keys share `head_share` of the mass; the rest is noisy background."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    w = [0.0] * n
    for i in range(head):
        w[i] = head_share / head * (0.8 + 0.4 * rng.random())
    for i in range(head, n):
        w[i] = (1.0 - head_share) / (n - head) * (0.5 + rng.random())
    return normalize(w)

# 1-2. Concentration floor and its sharpness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def concentration_floor(tau: float, p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    """Theorem: any k with M(k) >= tau obeys k >= tau^2 * eff(p)."""
    return tau * tau * eff_support(p)

def power_tail_mass_bound(c: float, alpha: float, k: int) -> float:
    """Guaranteed mass 1 - c/(alpha-1) * k^(1-alpha) under p_(i) <= c (i+1)^(-alpha)."""
    return 1.0 - c / (alpha - 1.0) * k ** (1.0 - alpha)


def power_tail_knee_ceiling(c: float, alpha: float, tau: float) -> float:
    """Sufficient width: (c / ((alpha-1)(1-tau)))^(1/(alpha-1))."""
    return (c / ((alpha - 1.0) * (1.0 - tau))) ** (1.0 / (alpha - 1.0))


def demo_tail_ceiling() -> None:

def exact_expected_random_mass(p: Sequence[float], k: int) -> float:
    """Brute-force average of captured mass over ALL k-subsets (small n only)."""
    n = len(p)
    idx = range(n)
    total = 0.0
    count = 0
    for S in itertools.combinations(idx, k):
        total += sum(p[i] for i in S)
        count += 1
    return total / count

# 5-7. Concavity, unimodality, peak
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_concave_sequence(f: Sequence[float], tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool:
    return all(f[k + 2] + f[k] <= 2.0 * f[k + 1] + tol for k in range(len(f) - 2))


def is_unimodal(f: Sequence[float], tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool:
    """min(f[i], f[m]) <= f[j] for all i <= j <= m (checked exhaustively)."""
    n = len(f)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            for m in range(j, n):
                if min(f[i], f[m]) > f[j] + tol:
                    return False
    return True


def chord_extrapolation(f_at_i: float, f_at_j: float, i: int, j: int, t: int) -> float:
    """Concavity cap on f(j+t) given f(i), f(j) with j - i = t."""
    if j - i != t:
        raise ValueError("chord comparison needs equal step lengths")
    return f_at_j + (f_at_j - f_at_i)

def demo_accuracy_transfer() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. ACCURACY TRANSFER:  concave response, Lipschitz ceiling L * TV")
    print("=" * 74)
    p = mixture_row(512, 180, 0.90, seed=11)
    M = mass_curve(p)
    scale, rate = 0.15, 3.0  # accuracy scale and saturation rate

    def g(x: float) -> float:
        """Concave nondecreasing response g(x) = scale * (1 - exp(-rate x)).

        Its derivative scale*rate*exp(-rate x) is positive and decreasing, so g is
        nondecreasing, concave, and Lipschitz with constant L = scale * rate.
        """
        x = min(max(x, 0.0), 1.0)
        return scale * (1.0 - math.exp(-rate * x))

    lipschitz = scale * rate
    acc = [g(m) for m in M]
    print(f"  response g(x) = {scale} (1 - e^(-{rate}x)): concave, nondecreasing,"
          f" L = {lipschitz:.3f}")
    print(f"  accuracy curve k -> g(M(k)) concave = {is_concave_sequence(acc)}")
    incs = [acc[k + 1] - acc[k] for k in range(len(acc) - 1)]
    print("  increments nonincreasing (diminishing returns) = "
          f"{all(incs[k + 1] <= incs[k] + 1e-12 for k in range(len(incs) - 1))}")
    tv = tv_to_uniform(p)
    worst = max(g(M[k]) - g(k / len(p)) for k in range(len(p) + 1))
    print(f"  TV(p, uniform) = {tv:.6f}")
    print(f"  max_k [ g(M(k)) - g(k/n) ] = {worst:.6f}"
          f"   <=  L * TV = {lipschitz * tv:.6f}   ->"
          f" {worst <= lipschitz * tv + 1e-12}")
    print(f"  width-free mass-gap cap  max_k G(k) = {max(selection_gap_curve(p)):.6f}"
          f"  (equals TV: {abs(max(selection_gap_curve(p)) - tv) < 1e-12})")

SWEEP_GRID: Tuple[int, ...] = (96, 128, 160, 192, 224, 240, 256, 288, 320, 384, 512)


def certified_bracket(grid: Sequence[int], passes: Callable[[int], bool]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Least passing grid point b and its predecessor a; the knee lies in (a, b]."""
    lo, hi = 0, len(grid) - 1
    if not passes(grid[hi]):
        raise ValueError("no grid point passes")
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if passes(grid[mid]):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    b = grid[lo]
    a = grid[lo - 1] if lo > 0 else 0
    return a, b


def grid_resolution(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    """(1 - 1/rho) * b with rho = b / a: the residual uncertainty of reporting b."""
    rho = b / a
    return (1.0 - 1.0 / rho) * b

    print(f"  grid points inside the bracket: {inside}  -> unique = {len(inside) == 1}")
    print(f"  => two seeds bracketed alike must report the same knee, k* = {b}")
    print(f"  resolution: |b - k*| <= (1 - 1/rho) b = {grid_resolution(a, b):.2f}"
          f"   with rho = {b}/{a} = {b / a:.6f}")
    print(f"  attained by the step curve r(k) = 1[k > {a}], whose true knee is {a + 1}")
    print()

import itertools
import random
from fractions import Fraction
from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple


def random_rational_row(n: int, rng: random.Random) -> List[Fraction]:
    """A random attention row with exactly representable rational weights."""
    raw = [Fraction(rng.randint(1, 40)) for _ in range(n)]
    total = sum(raw)
    return [x / total for x in raw]


def mass_curve(p: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    out = [Fraction(0)]
    acc = Fraction(0)
    for x in sorted(p, reverse=True):
        acc += x
        out.append(acc)
    return out


def gap_curve(p: Sequence[Fraction]) -> List[Fraction]:
    n = len(p)
    return [m - Fraction(k, n) for k, m in enumerate(mass_curve(p))]


def exact_random_mass(p: Sequence[Fraction], k: int) -> Fraction:
    """Average captured mass over ALL k-subsets, in exact arithmetic."""
    n = len(p)
    total = Fraction(0)
    count = 0
    for S in itertools.combinations(range(n), k):
        total += sum(p[i] for i in S)
        count += 1
    return total / count


def tv_to_uniform(p: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Fraction:
    n = len(p)
    return sum(abs(x - Fraction(1, n)) for x in p) / 2


def above_average(p: Sequence[Fraction]) -> int:
    n = len(p)
    return sum(1 for x in p if x > Fraction(1, n))


def audit_row(p: Sequence[Fraction]) -> Tuple[bool, bool, bool, bool]:
    n = len(p)
    M = mass_curve(p)
    G = gap_curve(p)

    control_exact = all(exact_random_mass(p, k) == Fraction(k, n)

    concave = all(M[k + 2] + M[k] <= 2 * M[k + 1] for k in range(n - 1))

    peak_ok = (G[peak] == G[above_average(p)]) and G[peak] == tv_to_uniform(p)
    ceiling_ok = all(g <= tv_to_uniform(p) for g in G)
    return control_exact, concave, peak_ok, ceiling_ok

def mass_and_gap_profile(p: Sequence[float]) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Compute the full top-k mass curve, the selection gap, and their invariants.

    Input:  p, an attention row (nonnegative, sums to 1) on n keys.
    Output: a dictionary containing

              'unimodal'  : whether the increments of G change sign at most once.

    srt = sorted(p, reverse=True)

    mass: List[float] = [0.0]
    acc = 0.0
    for x in srt:
        acc += x
        mass.append(acc)

    gap: List[float] = [mass[k] - k / n for k in range(n + 1)]

    eff = 1.0 / sum(x * x for x in p)
    tv = 0.5 * sum(abs(x - 1.0 / n) for x in p)

        "eff": eff,
        "tv": tv,
        "peak": peak,
        "above_avg": above_avg,
        "concave": concave,
        "unimodal": unimodal,
    }

from typing import Callable, Dict, Sequence


def certified_knee(grid: Sequence[int],
                   passes: Callable[[int], bool]) -> Dict[str, object]:
    """Locate the knee on a grid and report the bracket, resolution, and uniqueness.

    Assumes the pass predicate is upward closed (widening a passing budget still
    passes), which holds whenever the accuracy curve is nondecreasing in the width.

    Returns a dictionary with
      'fail_at'    : the largest grid point known to fail (0 if none was tested);
      'pass_at'    : the least passing grid point b, the reported knee;
      'bracket'    : the half-open interval (a, b] containing the true knee;
      'unique'     : whether b is the only grid point inside the bracket;
      'ratio'      : the local grid ratio rho = b / a;
      'resolution' : (1 - 1/rho) * b, the maximal absolute error of reporting b;
      'oracle_calls': number of pass-oracle evaluations used.

    Complexity: O(log |grid|) oracle calls by binary search, since the predicate is
    monotone along the sorted grid; O(1) additional space.
    """
    g = sorted(set(int(k) for k in grid))
    if not g:
        raise ValueError("empty grid")

    calls = 0

    def oracle(k: int) -> bool:
        nonlocal calls
        calls += 1
        return passes(k)

    if not oracle(g[-1]):
        raise ValueError("no grid point passes the bar; widen the grid")

    lo, hi = 0, len(g) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if oracle(g[mid]):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1

    b = g[lo]
    a = g[lo - 1] if lo > 0 else 0
    inside = [k for k in g if a < k <= b]
    rho = (b / a) if a > 0 else float("inf")
    resolution = (1.0 - 1.0 / rho) * b if a > 0 else float(b)

    return {
        "fail_at": a,
        "pass_at": b,
        "bracket": (a, b),
        "unique": len(inside) == 1,
        "ratio": rho,
        "resolution": resolution,
        "oracle_calls": calls,
    }

def fit_power_tail(p: Sequence[float],
                   alpha_grid: Sequence[float] = tuple(
                       1.05 + 0.05 * j for j in range(40))) -> Tuple[float, float]:
    """Fit a majorant p_(i) <= c (i+1)^(-alpha) to the descending sort of p.

    For each candidate exponent alpha, the smallest admissible constant is
    c(alpha) = max_i p_(i) (i+1)^alpha.  We select the exponent minimising the
    certified tail mass c(alpha)/(alpha-1), i.e. the tightest bound the family can
    deliver.  Complexity: O(|alpha_grid| * n) after one O(n log n) sort.
    """
    srt = sorted(p, reverse=True)
    n = len(srt)
    best: Tuple[float, float] = (float("inf"), 2.0)
    for alpha in alpha_grid:
        c = max(srt[i] * (i + 1.0) ** alpha for i in range(n))
        score = c / (alpha - 1.0)
        if score < best[0]:
            best = (score, alpha)
    alpha = best[1]
    c = max(srt[i] * (i + 1.0) ** alpha for i in range(n))
    return c, alpha


def knee_sandwich(p: Sequence[float], tau: float) -> Dict[str, float]:
    """Bound the minimal width reaching captured mass tau from both sides.

    Lower bound (concentration floor, from Cauchy-Schwarz):
        k >= tau^2 * eff(p),        eff(p) = 1 / sum_i p_i^2.
    Upper bound (power-tail ceiling, from a tangent-line tail estimate):
        k >= (c / ((alpha-1)(1-tau)))^(1/(alpha-1))  suffices,
    whenever p_(i) <= c (i+1)^(-alpha) with alpha > 1.

    Also returns the exact minimal width computed from the sorted row, which must
    lie inside the reported interval.  Complexity: O(n log n).
    """
    if not 0.0 <= tau < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("tau must lie in [0, 1)")
    n = len(p)
    eff = 1.0 / sum(x * x for x in p)
    floor = tau * tau * eff

    c, alpha = fit_power_tail(p)
    ceiling = (c / ((alpha - 1.0) * (1.0 - tau))) ** (1.0 / (alpha - 1.0))
    ceiling = min(ceiling, float(n))

    acc, exact = 0.0, n
    for k, x in enumerate(sorted(p, reverse=True), start=1):
        acc += x
        if acc >= tau:
            exact = k
            break

    return {
        "eff": eff,
        "floor": floor,
        "tail_c": c,
        "tail_alpha": alpha,
        "ceiling": ceiling,
        "exact_min_width": float(exact),
        "floor_valid": float(exact >= floor - 1e-9),
        "ceiling_valid": float(exact <= math.ceil(ceiling) + 1e-9),
    }

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def normalize(w: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    s = float(sum(w))
    return [x / s for x in w]


def power_row(n: int, alpha: float) -> List[float]:
    return normalize([(i + 1.0) ** (-alpha) for i in range(n)])


def mass_curve(p: Sequence[float]) -> List[float]:
    out, acc = [0.0], 0.0
    for x in sorted(p, reverse=True):
        acc += x
        out.append(acc)
    return out


def eff_support(p: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    return 1.0 / sum(x * x for x in p)


def tail_constant(p: Sequence[float], alpha: float) -> float:
    """Smallest c with p_(i) <= c (i+1)^(-alpha) for the descending sort of p."""
    srt = sorted(p, reverse=True)
    return max(srt[i] * (i + 1.0) ** alpha for i in range(len(srt)))


def knee_ceiling(c: float, alpha: float, tau: float) -> float:
    return (c / ((alpha - 1.0) * (1.0 - tau))) ** (1.0 / (alpha - 1.0))

    n, alpha, tau = 512, 1.3, 0.92
    p = power_row(n, alpha)
    M = mass_curve(p)
    e = eff_support(p)
    c = tail_constant(p, alpha)
    floor = tau * tau * e
    ceiling = knee_ceiling(c, alpha, tau)
    true_k = next(k for k in range(n + 1) if M[k] >= tau)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12.5, 8.6))

    ax[0][0].axvline(ceiling, ls="--", color="tab:blue", lw=1.6,
                     label=f"tail ceiling = {ceiling:.0f}")
    ax[0][0].axvline(true_k, color="k", lw=1.2, label=f"true minimal width = {true_k}")
    ax[0][0].set_title("(a) the knee is sandwiched")
    ax[0][0].set_xlabel("width k")
    ax[0][0].set_ylabel("captured mass")
    ax[0][0].legend(fontsize=8)
    ax[0][0].grid(alpha=0.25)

    taus = [0.50 + 0.01 * j for j in range(49)]
    floors = [t * t * e for t in taus]
    ceils = [knee_ceiling(c, alpha, t) for t in taus]
    trues = [next(k for k in range(n + 1) if M[k] >= t) for t in taus]
    ax[0][1].plot(taus, floors, lw=2, color="tab:red", label="floor τ²·eff")
    ax[0][1].plot(taus, trues, lw=2, color="k", label="true minimal width")
    ax[0][1].plot(taus, ceils, lw=2, color="tab:blue", label="tail ceiling")
    ax[0][1].fill_between(taus, floors, ceils, alpha=0.12, color="tab:blue")

<script>
const $ = id => document.getElementById(id);

function buildRow(){
  const kind = $('profile').value;
  const n = +$('n').value, alpha = +$('alpha').value;
  const head = Math.min(+$('head').value, n), share = +$('share').value;
  let w = new Array(n).fill(0);
  if(kind === 'power'){
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++) w[i] = Math.pow(i+1, -alpha);
  } else if(kind === 'uniform'){
    w.fill(1);
  } else if(kind === 'spike'){
    w.fill((1-share)/(n-1)); w[0] = share;
  } else {
    for(let i=0;i<n;i++){
      const t = i < head ? share/head : (1-share)/Math.max(1,n-head);
      // deterministic pseudo-noise so the picture is stable while dragging
      const jitter = 0.75 + 0.5*Math.abs(Math.sin(1.7*i + 0.3));
      w[i] = t*jitter;
    }
  }
  const s = w.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);
  return w.map(x=>x/s);
}

function analyse(p){
  const n = p.length;
  const srt = [...p].sort((a,b)=>b-a);
  const M = [0];
  let acc = 0;
  for(const x of srt){ acc += x; M.push(acc); }
  const G = M.map((m,k)=> m - k/n);
  const sumSq = p.reduce((a,x)=>a+x*x,0);
  const eff = 1/sumSq;
  const tv = 0.5*p.reduce((a,x)=>a+Math.abs(x-1/n),0);
  const above = p.filter(x=>x>1/n).length;
  let peak = 0; for(let k=0;k<=n;k++) if(G[k] > G[peak]) peak = k;
  return {n, M, G, eff, tv, above, peak, srt};
}

function draw(canvas, series, opts){
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  const W = canvas.width, H = canvas.height, pad = {l:52,r:14,t:14,b:28};
  ctx.clearRect(0,0,W,H);
  ctx.fillStyle = '#0c1020'; ctx.fillRect(0,0,W,H);
  const n = opts.n, ymin = opts.ymin, ymax = opts.ymax;
  const X = k => pad.l + (W-pad.l-pad.r)*k/n;
  const Y = v => H-pad.b - (H-pad.t-pad.b)*(v-ymin)/(ymax-ymin);
  // grid
  ctx.strokeStyle = '#1d2440'; ctx.lineWidth = 1; ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace';
  ctx.fillStyle = '#6c7699';
  for(let g=0; g<=4; g++){
    const v = ymin + (ymax-ymin)*g/4, y = Y(v);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(pad.l,y); ctx.lineTo(W-pad.r,y); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillText(v.toFixed(2), 8, y+4);
  }
  for(let g=0; g<=4; g++){
    const k = Math.round(n*g/4), x = X(k);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x,pad.t); ctx.lineTo(x,H-pad.b); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillText(String(k), x-10, H-9);
  }
  for(const s of series){
    ctx.strokeStyle = s.color; ctx.lineWidth = s.width||2;
    ctx.setLineDash(s.dash||[]);
    ctx.beginPath();
    s.data.forEach((v,k)=>{ const x=X(k), y=Y(v); k? ctx.lineTo(x,y) : ctx.moveTo(x,y); });
    ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);
    if(s.fill){
      ctx.lineTo(X(n), Y(ymin)); ctx.lineTo(X(0), Y(ymin)); ctx.closePath();
      ctx.fillStyle = s.fill; ctx.fill();
    }
  }
  for(const m of (opts.marks||[])){
    if(m.k < 0 || m.k > n) continue;
    ctx.strokeStyle = m.color; ctx.lineWidth = 2; ctx.setLineDash([5,4]);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(m.k), pad.t); ctx.lineTo(X(m.k), H-pad.b); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.setLineDash([]);
    ctx.fillStyle = m.color; ctx.font = '11px ui-monospace,monospace';
    ctx.fillText(m.label, Math.min(X(m.k)+5, W-pad.r-90), pad.t+12+(m.row||0)*13);
  }
}

function stat(k,v,cls){ return `<div class="stat"><div class="k">${k}</div>
  <div class="v ${cls||''}">${v}</div></div>`; }

  "interactive_layout": "# How Narrow Can Attention Be?

### A guided tour of the geometry behind top-$k$ attention

> **The one-sentence version.** Keeping only the $k$ heaviest entries of an attention row is
> governed by four elementary facts — a Cauchy–Schwarz floor, a tail-decay ceiling, an exact
> $k/n$ baseline, and a one-move exchange argument that makes everything concave — and together
> they explain why, at depth $32$ and context $512$, the honest width is $256$ and the honest
> speedup is exactly $2.0\times$.

---

## 1. The marble problem

Imagine a bag of $n$ numbered marbles. Marble $i$ carries weight $p_i \ge 0$, and the weights sum
to one. You may keep only $k$ of them. Which do you keep, and how much weight do you save?

Keeping the heaviest $k$ is obviously optimal. The interesting quantity is *how much* that buys:

$$M(k) \;=\; \max_{|S| \le k} \sum_{i \in S} p_i .$$

This is not a toy. It is exactly what happens inside the attention mechanism of a language model:
each position produces a probability vector over the earlier positions, and *top-$k$ attention*
keeps only the $k$ largest entries. The cost falls from $n \cdot n$ to $n \cdot k$ — a speedup of
$n/k$ — and the question is how small $k$ can get before accuracy suffers. That threshold width is
called the **knee**, $k^{*}$.

<details>
<summary><b>Notation, once and for all</b> (click to expand)</summary>

- $p = (p_1,\dots,p_n)$: an **attention row**, $p_i \ge 0$, $\sum_i p_i = 1$.
- $M(k)$: the **top-$k$ captured mass**, the sum of the $k$ largest weights.
- $\mathrm{eff}(p) = 1/\sum_i p_i^2$: the **effective support**, or
  [participation ratio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse_participation_ratio). It equals $n$
  for the uniform row and $1$ for a point mass.
- $G(k) = M(k) - k/n$: the **selection gap** — how much better choosing well is than choosing blind.
- $\mathrm{TV}(p,\mathrm{unif}) = \tfrac12\sum_i |p_i - 1/n|$: the
  [total-variation distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_variation_distance_of_probability_measures)
  to uniform attention.
- $\mathrm{ctx}$: the context length; the top-$k$ speedup is $\mathrm{ctx}/k$.
</details>

---

## 2. Play with it first

Before any proofs, get the picture in your hands. Shape an attention row and watch the mass curve,
the gap, the floor and the ceiling move together. Everything in the "live theorem check" panel is a
statement we prove below — if any box ever turns red, the mathematics would be wrong.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

Three things to try:

1. **Slide the tail exponent $\alpha$ down toward $0.6$.** The row flattens, the effective support
   grows, the floor marches right, and the knee follows it. Concentration is not optional.
2. **Watch the peak marker in the lower chart.** It always sits at the number of above-average keys,
   and its height always equals the total-variation distance. That is Section 5.
3. **Set the profile to uniform.** The gap collapses to zero everywhere: with nothing to choose
   between, selection is worthless — exactly as $\mathrm{TV} = 0$ predicts.

---

## 3. From below: you cannot be too greedy

Here is the first hard constraint, and it takes one line.

Let $S$ be the optimal width-$k$ set. Then
[Cauchy–Schwarz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cauchy%E2%80%93Schwarz_inequality) gives
$M(k)^2 = \big(\sum_{i\in S} p_i\big)^2 \le |S| \sum_{i \in S} p_i^2 \le k \sum_i p_i^2$, so:

$$\textbf{Concentration floor:}\qquad M(k) \ge \tau \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; k \;\ge\; \tau^2 \cdot \mathrm{eff}(p).$$

No selection rule — greedy, learned, or oracular — escapes this. At the measured cell the effective
support is $\approx 216.92$ and the top-$256$ mass is $0.922$, so any width reaching mass $0.92$ must
exceed $0.92^2 \times 216.92 > 183$. A measured knee of $256$ is corroborated; a claimed knee of $96$
is refuted outright.

<details>
<summary><b>Is the square in $\tau^2$ just a lazy proof?</b> No — here is the counterexample.</summary>

Take the five-key profile $q = (\tfrac12, \tfrac18, \tfrac18, \tfrac18, \tfrac18)$. Then
$\sum q_i^2 = \tfrac14 + 4\cdot\tfrac1{64} = \tfrac5{16}$, so $\mathrm{eff}(q) = \tfrac{16}{5} = 3.2$,
and a single key already captures $\tau = \tfrac12$.

- Proved floor: $\tau^2 \mathrm{eff} = 0.8 \le 1$. ✓
- Tempting "improvement": $\tau\,\mathrm{eff} = 1.6 > 1$. ✗ — false.

So the exponent $2$ cannot be raised to $1$. Conversely the floor is *loose* on flat rows: for the
uniform row the true minimal width is $\lceil \tau n\rceil$ while the floor only certifies
$\tau^2 n$, a slack factor $1/\tau$.
</details>

---

## 4. From above: tails are forgiving

Suppose the sorted weights decay like a power law, $p_{(i)} \le c\,i^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha > 1$.
Summing the tail gives the complementary bound:

$$M(k) \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{c}{\alpha-1}\,k^{1-\alpha}, \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
k^{*} \;\le\; \Big(\frac{c}{(\alpha-1)(1-\tau)}\Big)^{1/(\alpha-1)} .$$

<details>
<summary><b>The analytic engine: a tangent-line step (Bernoulli in disguise)</b></summary>

For $\alpha = 2$ the tail sum telescopes exactly, because $\sum_{j \ge k}(j+1)^{-2} \le 1/k$ follows
from $\frac{1}{(j+1)^2} \le \frac1j - \frac1{j+1}$. For general real $\alpha$ nothing telescopes, and
the substitute is

$$(\alpha-1)(x+1)^{-\alpha} \;\le\; x^{1-\alpha} - (x+1)^{1-\alpha}, \qquad x \ge 1,\ \alpha > 1 .$$

Read the right-hand side as $\int_x^{x+1}(\alpha-1)t^{-\alpha}\,dt$ and use that $t^{-\alpha}$ is
decreasing; or, with no integration at all, recognise
[Bernoulli's inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_inequality)
$1 + \alpha s \le (1+s)^{\alpha}$ at $s = 1/x$. Convexity supplies exactly the slack that exact
telescoping supplies for free at $\alpha = 2$. Telescoping the step over $x = k, \dots, n-1$ gives
$\sum_{j\ge k}(j+1)^{-\alpha} \le \frac{k^{1-\alpha}}{\alpha-1}$, and the mass bound follows by taking
$S$ to be the top-ranked $k$ keys.
</details>

Two instances at $n = 512$, both certifying the measured top-$256$ mass of $0.922$: an inverse-square
tail with $c = 20$ gives $M(256) \ge 1 - 20/256 \ge 0.92$; the much heavier tail $\alpha = 3/2$ with
$c = 0.6$ gives $M(256) \ge 1 - 1.2/16 = 0.925$. Heavy tails do not break the story — they change
only the rate.

## 5. Is top-$k$ actually doing anything? The control that math settles exactly

Every sparsification claim owes its reader a control: what if we picked $k$ keys *at random*?

Average the captured mass over all $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$. Each key lies in
$\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ of them, so the total is $\binom{n-1}{k-1}$ and the average is

$$\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{i \in R} p_i\Big] \;=\; \frac{\binom{n-1}{k-1}}{\binom{n}{k}} \;=\; \frac{k}{n}.$$

Exactly $k/n$ — **independently of the attention row**. That is what makes the random control a
legitimate baseline, and it is why the selection gap is defined as $G(k) = M(k) - k/n$. At the
measured cell, $M(256) = 0.922$ against a baseline of $0.5$: a mass gap of at least $0.42$.

Do not take the identity on faith — enumerate it in exact rational arithmetic:

{{demo:1}}

### The shape of the gap: one exchange move

Why does the gap dilute *smoothly* as $k$ grows? Because the mass curve is concave, and the proof is
a single move.

<details>
<summary><b>The exchange argument in full</b></summary>

Let $S$ be optimal of size $\le k+2$ and $T$ optimal of size $\le k$.

*Case 1: $|S| \le k+1$.* Then both sets are admissible at width $k+1$, so
$M(k+2) \le M(k+1)$ and $M(k) \le M(k+1)$; add them.

*Case 2: $|S| = k+2$.* Then $|S| > |T|$, so there is a key $x \in S \setminus T$. Move it:
$S\setminus\{x\}$ and $T\cup\{x\}$ both have size at most $k+1$, and

$$\Big(\sum_S p - p_x\Big) + \Big(p_x + \sum_T p\Big) \;=\; M(k+2) + M(k),$$

with each bracket at most $M(k+1)$. Hence $M(k+2) + M(k) \le 2M(k+1)$: the mass curve is a **concave
sequence**. Subtracting the straight line $k/n$ preserves this, so the gap is concave too.
</details>

Concave sequences have nonincreasing increments, so they rise and then fall: they are **unimodal**,
meaning $\min(G(i), G(m)) \le G(j)$ whenever $i \le j \le m$. And since $G(0) = 0$ and $G(n) = 0$ —
at full width, "best" and "random" both take everything — unimodality *re-derives* $G(k) \ge 0$ from
shape alone. Two entirely different proofs (a double count and a shape argument) of the same fact.

Concavity also makes a **falsifiable prediction**: a concave curve cannot decay slower later than
earlier, so measured gaps of $+2.6$ at $k = 256$ and $+1.7$ at $k = 384$ force the gap at $k = 512$
to be at most $+0.8$. Measure more than that and concavity of the accuracy gap is refuted.

---

## 6. Where the peak sits — and why it is a classical distance

If the gap rises and falls, it has a top. Call a key **above average** if $p_i > 1/n$, and let $A$ be
the set of such keys. Then:

$$\boxed{\ \arg\max_k G(k) = |A|, \qquad \max_k G(k) = \sum_i \Big(p_i - \tfrac1n\Big)^{+} = \mathrm{TV}(p,\mathrm{unif}).\ }$$

<details>
<summary><b>Proof in three lines</b></summary>

For any set $S$: $\sum_{i\in S} p_i - \frac{|S|}{n} = \sum_{i \in S}(p_i - \frac1n) \le \sum_i (p_i - \frac1n)^+ =: E(p)$.
Since $|S| \le k$ for admissible $S$, this gives $G(k) \le E(p)$ for every width — a **width-free
ceiling**. Taking $S = A$ attains it, because off $A$ the positive part vanishes. Finally, the signed
deviations $p_i - 1/n$ sum to zero, so the positive and negative parts are equal and each is half the
$\ell^1$ deviation: $E(p) = \tfrac12\sum_i|p_i - \frac1n| = \mathrm{TV}(p,\mathrm{unif})$.
</details>

Three consequences worth savouring:

- **No scheme beats the distance.** *Any* selection rule, at *any* width, beats the random control by
  at most $\mathrm{TV}(p,\mathrm{unif})$ in captured mass.
- **A second floor on the knee.** Rearranging, $M(k)\ge\tau$ forces $k \ge n(\tau - \mathrm{TV})$:
  rows close to uniform cannot have small knees, whatever their participation ratio.
- **The measurement, restated.** Top-$256$ mass $0.922$ at $n = 512$ forces
  $\mathrm{TV} \ge 0.922 - 0.5 = 0.422$.

diagonal, over eighty different profiles:

And here is the routine that computes the whole profile, returning concavity and unimodality as
verifiable certificates:

{{algorithm:0}}

### From mass to accuracy

The measured quantity is accuracy, not captured mass. One hypothesis bridges them: *accuracy is a
concave nondecreasing function $g$ of captured mass*. Then $k \mapsto g(M(k))$ is itself concave —
hence unimodal, with diminishing returns per unit of width, exactly the shape a knee sweep
presupposes. And if $g$ is $L$-Lipschitz, the accuracy gap against the random control is at most
$L \cdot \mathrm{TV}(p,\mathrm{unif})$, uniformly in $k$. One classical distance caps the entire
control experiment.

---

## 7. Reading a knee off a grid, honestly

A sweep tests finitely many widths. Because widening a passing budget still passes, the pass
predicate is **upward closed**, the knee is the least passing width, and a fail at $a$ with a pass at
$b$ pins it to $(a, b]$. In the round in question, width $240$ failed (ratio $0.978$ against a bar of
$0.98$) and width $256$ passed ($0.982$), giving the bracket $(240, 256]$.

Now the crucial remark: on the grid $\{96, 128, 160, 192, 224, 240, 256, 288, 320, 384, 512\}$, that
bracket contains **exactly one** grid point. So two seeds that both fail at $240$ and pass at $256$
*must* report the same knee. "Exact reproduction" is, at this resolution, a theorem about the grid —
which is precisely why the residual uncertainty must be reported too: with local ratio
$\rho = 256/240 = 16/15$, reporting $256$ carries up to $(1-1/\rho)\cdot 256 = 16$ of absolute error,
and that bound is *attained* by a step-shaped accuracy curve whose true knee is $241$.

## 8. The depth law and the payoff

Sweeping the knee across model depths $d$ produced a concave fit $k^{*}(d) \approx 24.7\,d^{2/3}$
against two rivals: an affine law $8d + 32$ and a product law $k^{*} = \mathrm{ctx}$.

| law | prediction at $d = 32$ | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| concave $24.7\,d^{2/3}$ | $248.96 \in (248.9, 249)$ | within $3\%$ of the measured $256$ |
| affine $8d + 32$ | $288$ | over-predicts by more than $11\%$ |
| product $k = \mathrm{ctx}$ | $512$ | wrong by a factor of $2$ |

The affine failure is *structural*, not accidental: an affine function calibrated on two points of a
concave curve necessarily lies above the curve when extrapolated outward. The concave law's
signature is its per-doubling factor $2^{2/3} \in (1.58, 1.59)$, comfortably below $2$; and the three
measured per-doubling ratios $1.50$, $1.58$, $1.68$ have product $3.9816$, implying an empirical
exponent $a$ with $2^{3a} = 3.9816$, i.e. $0.6 < a < 2/3$ — sub-linear, just under the fitted
envelope.

<details>
<summary><b>Why $0.6 < a < 2/3$, by hand</b></summary>

Upper: $3.9816 < 4 = 2^2$, and $x \mapsto 2^x$ is increasing, so $3a < 2$.
Lower: $\big(2^{9/5}\big)^5 = 2^9 = 512$ while $3.98^5 \approx 998 > 512$, so $2^{9/5} < 3.9816$ and
$3a > 9/5$. Hence $0.6 < a < 2/3$.
</details>

Finally, the payoff is pure arithmetic. Top-$k$ attention at context $\mathrm{ctx}$ costs
$\mathrm{ctx}\cdot k$, so the speedup is $\mathrm{ctx}/k$:

- product law, $k = 512$: speedup $= 1.000$ — **no saving at all**;
- measured knee, $k = 256$: speedup $= 512/256 = \mathbf{2.0\times}$, at both seeds;
- and any knee at most half the context is worth at least a doubling.

---

## 9. Run the whole thing

Every claim above, instantiated on concrete attention rows and checked numerically — floors,
ceilings, the exact $k/n$ control, concavity, unimodality, the peak identity, the Lipschitz ceiling,
the bracket, the depth law and the speedup:

{{demo:0}}

---

## 10. What the mathematics is for

None of the measured numbers can be proved; they are measurements. What *can* be proved — and is —
are the structural laws that make the protocol mean something:

- top-$k$ is optimal, and any control missing a heavier key is strictly worse;
- the random control's expected mass is exactly $k/n$, whatever the row;
- the mass curve is concave, so the gap is concave, unimodal, nonnegative, and vanishes at full width;
- the gap peaks at the above-average keys, at a height equal to a total-variation distance;
- concentration floors and tail ceilings sandwich the knee;
- an exactly reproducing knee on a coarse grid is a grid theorem with a stated, attained resolution;
- a concave depth law forces affine extrapolation to over-predict.

The experiment supplies the numbers. The mathematics supplies the reasons the numbers can be trusted,
the shape they must have, and the next prediction that could knock the whole picture down.

* the **grid resolution bound** `|b − k| ≤ (1 − 1/ρ) · b` (`knee_grid_resolution`).

open Finset

/-! ## A. The uniform profile: exact top-`k` mass and the slack in the floor -/

/-- The uniform attention profile on `n` keys. -/
noncomputable def uniformDist (n : ℕ) (hn : 0 < n) : AttnDist n where
  p := fun _ => 1 / n
  nonneg := fun _ => by positivity
  sum_one := by
    have hnR : (n : ℝ) ≠ 0 := Nat.cast_ne_zero.2 hn.ne'
    simp [Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ]
    field_simp

/-- **Closed form.**  For the uniform profile the best width-`k` selection captures exactly
`k / n` of the mass. -/
theorem bestMass_uniform {n k : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hkn : k ≤ n) :
    bestMass (uniformDist n hn) k = (k : ℝ) / n := by
  have hnR : (0:ℝ) < (n : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hn
  refine le_antisymm ?_ ?_
  · refine Finset.sup'_le _ _ (fun S hS => ?_)
    have hcard : (S.card : ℝ) ≤ (k : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast mem_Kset.1 hS
    have : ∑ _i ∈ S, (1 : ℝ) / n = (S.card : ℝ) / n := by
      rw [Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul]
      ring
    simp only [uniformDist]
    rw [this]
    exact (div_le_div_iff_of_pos_right hnR).mpr hcard
  · obtain ⟨S, _, hScard⟩ := Finset.exists_subset_card_eq
      (show k ≤ (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).card by simpa using hkn)
    have h2 := mass_le_bestMass (uniformDist n hn) (S := S) (le_of_eq hScard)
    have h3 : ∑ i ∈ S, (uniformDist n hn).p i = (k : ℝ) / n := by
      simp only [uniformDist]
      rw [Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul, hScard]
      ring
    rw [h3] at h2
    exact h2

/-- The effective support of the uniform profile is `n`. -/
theorem eff_uniform {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) : eff (uniformDist n hn) = (n : ℝ) := by
  have hnR : (0:ℝ) < (n : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast hn
  have hsq : sumSq (uniformDist n hn) = 1 / n := by
    simp only [sumSq, uniformDist, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin,
      nsmul_eq_mul]
    field_simp
  rw [eff, hsq, one_div_one_div]

exactly the factor `τ`. -/
theorem uniform_floor_slack {n k : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) (hkn : k ≤ n) {τ : ℝ}

  · nlinarith [mul_pos (mul_pos hτ0 hnR) (sub_pos.2 hτ1)]
  · rw [bestMass_uniform hn hkn, le_div_iff₀ hnR] at hpass
    linarith

/-- The spike profile `(1/2, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8, 1/8)` on five keys. -/
noncomputable def spikeDist : AttnDist 5 where
  p := fun i => if i = 0 then 1/2 else 1/8
  nonneg := fun i => by split <;> norm_num
  sum_one := by
    simp only [Fin.sum_univ_five]
    norm_num [Fin.ext_iff]

  simp only [sumSq, spikeDist, Fin.sum_univ_five]
  norm_num [Fin.ext_iff]

lemma spikeDist_eff : eff spikeDist = 16 / 5 := by
  rw [eff, spikeDist_sumSq]
  norm_num

  refine le_antisymm ?_ ?_
  · refine Finset.sup'_le _ _ (fun S hS => ?_)
    have hcard : S.card ≤ 1 := mem_Kset.1 hS
    rcases Finset.card_le_one.1 hcard with hone
    rcases S.eq_empty_or_nonempty with rfl | ⟨i, hi⟩
    · norm_num
    · have hSeq : S = {i} := Finset.eq_singleton_iff_unique_mem.2 ⟨hi, fun x hx => hone x hx i hi⟩
      rw [hSeq, Finset.sum_singleton]
      fin_cases i <;> simp [spikeDist] <;> norm_num
  · have h := mass_le_bestMass (k := 1) spikeDist (S := ({0} : Finset (Fin 5))) (by simp)
    simpa [spikeDist] using h

/-- The adversarial accuracy curve: everything above `a` passes, everything up to `a` fails. -/
noncomputable def stepCurve (a : ℕ) : ℕ → ℝ := fun k => if a < k then 1 else 0

lemma stepCurve_monotone (a : ℕ) : Monotone (stepCurve a) := by
  intro x y hxy
  by_cases hx : a < x
  · simp [stepCurve, hx, lt_of_lt_of_le hx hxy]
  · simp only [stepCurve, if_neg hx]

    Monotone (stepCurve a) ∧ stepCurve a a < 1 ∧ (1:ℝ) ≤ stepCurve a b ∧
      knee (fun k => (1:ℝ) ≤ stepCurve a k) ⟨b, by simp [stepCurve, hab]⟩ = a + 1 := by

  push_neg at hcon

      ≤ knee (fun k => τ ≤ bestMass b k) hb :=
  knee_le _ (le_trans (knee_spec (fun k => τ ≤ bestMass b k) hb) (hdom _))

* `bestMass_ge_of_inverse_square_tail`
* `tail_ceiling`
* `knee_sandwich`
* `net43_tail_ceiling_at_256`

  have hx1 : (0:ℝ) < x + 1 := by linarith
  set A : ℝ := x ^ α with hA
  set B : ℝ := (x + 1) ^ α with hB
  have hApos : 0 < A := Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hx0 α

  have hs : (-1 : ℝ) ≤ 1 / x := by

    linarith
  have hbern : 1 + α * (1 / x) ≤ (1 + 1 / x) ^ α :=
    one_add_mul_self_le_rpow_one_add hs hα.le
  have hrw : (1 + 1 / x) ^ α = B / A := by
    have h1 : 1 + 1 / x = (x + 1) / x := by field_simp
    rw [h1, Real.div_rpow hx1.le hx0.le]

  have hkey : (α + x) * A ≤ x * B := by
    have h2 : (1 + α * (1 / x)) * A ≤ (B / A) * A :=

    rw [div_mul_cancel₀ _ (ne_of_gt hApos)] at h2
    have h3 : (1 + α * (1 / x)) * A * x ≤ B * x := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right h2 hx0.le
    have h4 : (1 + α * (1 / x)) * A * x = (x + α) * A := by
      field_simp
    rw [h4] at h3
    nlinarith [h3]

  have e1 : x ^ (1 - α) = x / A := by
    rw [Real.rpow_sub hx0, Real.rpow_one, hA]
  have e2 : (x + 1) ^ (1 - α) = (x + 1) / B := by
    rw [Real.rpow_sub hx1, Real.rpow_one, hB]
  have e3 : (x + 1) ^ (-α) = 1 / B := by
    rw [Real.rpow_neg hx1.le, hB, one_div]
  rw [e1, e2, e3]

    field_simp

    have hn : (0:ℝ) < (n : ℝ) := by exact_mod_cast lt_of_lt_of_le hk h.le
    have hpos : (0:ℝ) < (n : ℝ) ^ (1 - α) := Real.rpow_pos_of_pos hn _
    have hkey := key n h.le
    rw [le_div_iff₀ hα1]
    nlinarith [hkey, hpos]

/-! ## 2. The combinatorial half, for an arbitrary majorant -/

/-- **Mass captured by the top of a ranking.**  If the keys ranked at positions `≥ k` carry
total weight at most `B` (majorised term by term by `g`), then the top-`k` selection captures
mass at least `1 − B`.  This isolates the re-indexing argument of cycle 4 from the particular
inverse-square estimate. -/
theorem bestMass_ge_of_tail_bound {n : ℕ} (a : AttnDist n) (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin n))
    (g : ℕ → ℝ) (hdecay : ∀ i : Fin n, a.p (σ i) ≤ g i) {k : ℕ} {B : ℝ}
    (hB : ∑ j ∈ Finset.Ico k n, g j ≤ B) : 1 - B ≤ bestMass a k := by

  set S : Finset (Fin n) := Finset.univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => ((σ.symm x : Fin n) : ℕ) < k)
    with hS
  have hcard : S.card ≤ k := by
    have hinj : Set.InjOn (fun x : Fin n => ((σ.symm x : Fin n) : ℕ)) S := by
      intro x _ y _ hxy
      have : σ.symm x = σ.symm y := Fin.ext hxy
      simpa using congrArg σ this
    have hmaps : Set.MapsTo (fun x : Fin n => ((σ.symm x : Fin n) : ℕ)) ↑S ↑(Finset.range k) := by
      intro x hx
      have hx' : x ∈ S := hx
      simp only [hS, Finset.mem_filter] at hx'
      simpa using hx'.2
    have := Finset.card_le_card_of_injOn _ hmaps hinj
    simpa using this
  have hsplit : ∑ x ∈ S, a.p x + ∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter
      (fun x : Fin n => ¬ ((σ.symm x : Fin n) : ℕ) < k), a.p x = 1 := by
    rw [Finset.sum_filter_add_sum_filter_not]
    exact a.sum_one
  have hreindex : ∑ x ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => ¬ ((σ.symm x : Fin n) : ℕ) < k),
      a.p x = ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun j : Fin n => ¬ ((j : ℕ) < k)), a.p (σ j) := by
    refine (Finset.sum_equiv σ ?_ ?_).symm
    · intro j
      simp
    · intro j _
      rfl
  have htail : ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun j : Fin n => ¬ ((j : ℕ) < k)), a.p (σ j) ≤ B := by
    have hbound : ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun j : Fin n => ¬ ((j : ℕ) < k)), a.p (σ j)
        ≤ ∑ j ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun j : Fin n => ¬ ((j : ℕ) < k)), g (j : ℕ) :=
      Finset.sum_le_sum (fun j _ => hdecay j)
    have hset : (Finset.range n).filter (fun j : ℕ => ¬ (j < k)) = Finset.Ico k n := by
      ext j

        = ∑ j ∈ Finset.Ico k n, g j := by
      rw [Finset.sum_filter,
        Fin.sum_univ_eq_sum_range (fun j : ℕ => if ¬ (j < k) then g j else 0) n,
        ← Finset.sum_filter, hset]
    exact le_trans hbound (le_trans (le_of_eq hcast) hB)
  have hmass : 1 - B ≤ ∑ x ∈ S, a.p x := by
    rw [hreindex] at hsplit
    linarith
  exact le_trans hmass (mass_le_bestMass a hcard)

    _ = c / (α - 1) * (k : ℝ) ^ (1 - α) := by ring

    (hdecay : ∀ i : Fin n, a.p (σ i) ≤ c * ((((i : ℕ) : ℝ)) + 1) ^ (-α))

  have hτ1 : (0:ℝ) < 1 - τ := by linarith

    nlinarith [this]

open Classical in
/-- The **above-average keys**: those carrying strictly more than the uniform share `1/n`. -/
noncomputable def aboveAvg (a : AttnDist n) : Finset (Fin n) :=

    exact max_eq_right (by linarith [not_lt.1 this])

theorem selectionGap_aboveAvg (a : AttnDist n) (hn : 0 < n) :

    rw [Finset.sum_sub_distrib, Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul]

  have h1 : τ - excessMass a ≤ (k : ℝ) / n := by linarith

    exact (Finset.mem_filter.1 this).2

    mul_one_div, div_self hne] at hsum
  exact lt_irrefl _ hsum

/-! ## 2. Concavity transfer: from captured mass to accuracy -/

/-- **Concavity transfer.**  Post-composing a concave sequence with a concave nondecreasing
function again gives a concave sequence.  This is the formal content of "accuracy is a
concave increasing function of captured mass". -/
theorem ConcaveSeq.comp_concave {f : ℕ → ℝ} (hf : ConcaveSeq f) {g : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hg : ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ g) (hmono : Monotone g) : ConcaveSeq (fun k => g (f k)) := by
  intro k
  have hmid : (1 / 2 : ℝ) * f (k + 2) + (1 / 2 : ℝ) * f k ≤ f (k + 1) := by
    have := hf k; linarith
  have h1 := hg.2 (Set.mem_univ (f (k + 2))) (Set.mem_univ (f k))
    (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 1 / 2) (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 1 / 2) (by norm_num)
  simp only [smul_eq_mul] at h1
  have h2 : g ((1 / 2 : ℝ) * f (k + 2) + (1 / 2 : ℝ) * f k) ≤ g (f (k + 1)) := hmono hmid
  show g (f (k + 2)) + g (f k) ≤ 2 * g (f (k + 1))
  linarith

/-- **The accuracy curve is concave.**  With accuracy a concave nondecreasing function of
captured mass, the sweep's accuracy-versus-width curve is a concave sequence. -/
theorem accuracyCurve_concave (a : AttnDist n) {g : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hg : ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ g) (hmono : Monotone g) :
    ConcaveSeq (fun k => g (bestMass a k)) :=
  ConcaveSeq.comp_concave (fun k => bestMass_midpoint_concave a k) hg hmono

    (hg : ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ g) (hmono : Monotone g) {i j m : ℕ}
    (hij : i ≤ j) (hjm : j ≤ m) :
    min (g (bestMass a i)) (g (bestMass a m)) ≤ g (bestMass a j) :=
  (accuracyCurve_concave a hg hmono).min_le_of_between hij hjm

/-- The accuracy curve has antitone increments: each extra unit of width buys no more than
the previous one did. -/
theorem accuracyCurve_diff_antitone (a : AttnDist n) {g : ℝ → ℝ}
    (hg : ConcaveOn ℝ Set.univ g) (hmono : Monotone g) :
    Antitone (fun k => g (bestMass a (k + 1)) - g (bestMass a k)) :=

    rw [selectionGap] at this
    linarith

    have := selectionGap_le_excessMass a hn k
    rw [selectionGap] at this
    exact this

        hlip _ _ hxy
    _ ≤ L * excessMass a := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left hgap hL

/-! ## A. The random-`k` control -/

/-- The number of `k`-element subsets containing a fixed key is `C(n-1, k-1)`. -/
lemma card_powersetCard_filter_mem {k : ℕ} (hk : 1 ≤ k) (i : Fin n) :
    (((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).powersetCard k).filter (fun S => i ∈ S)).card
      = (n - 1).choose (k - 1) := by
  classical
  have key : (((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).powersetCard k).filter (fun S => i ∈ S)).card

    refine Finset.card_bij' (fun S _ => S.erase i) (fun T _ => insert i T) ?_ ?_ ?_ ?_
    · intro S hS
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powersetCard] at hS
      simp only [Finset.mem_powersetCard]
      refine ⟨Finset.erase_subset_erase _ hS.1.1, ?_⟩
      rw [Finset.card_erase_of_mem hS.2, hS.1.2]
    · intro T hT
      simp only [Finset.mem_powersetCard] at hT
      have hiT : i ∉ T := fun h => (Finset.mem_erase.1 (hT.1 h)).1 rfl
      simp only [Finset.mem_filter, Finset.mem_powersetCard]
      refine ⟨⟨Finset.subset_univ _, ?_⟩, Finset.mem_insert_self _ _⟩
      rw [Finset.card_insert_of_notMem hiT, hT.2]

      simp only [Finset.mem_filter] at hS
      exact Finset.insert_erase hS.2
